writing.title: We Were Never Asking for a Revolution
writing.description: A personal essay that moves between the legend of a burning convent and everyday life to explore queer storytelling, self-censorship and the freedom to be ordinary.

image.alt: Two women flee hand in hand from a burning convent at night

sample.audience: Readers of queer literature, personal essays and cultural commentary.
sample.objective: Use the legend of Julie d’Aubigny to ask why queer love so often has to be extraordinary to be told.

extracts.label: From the published essay
extracts.text: There is something terribly romantic about a woman who would burn down a convent for the person she loves. There is something considerably less romantic about a world in which she had to.

sample.notes: I move between the convent legend and ordinary scenes from my own life. That shift gives the essay its tension and reflects the Journal’s interest in personal writing and queer literature. The burning-convent artwork carried the opening image into the social campaign.

image.alt: Cold Feet Editions Pinterest designs for poetry gifts and literary products

sample.audience: People looking for gift ideas for a poetry lover, including readers unfamiliar with the studio.
sample.objective: Give shoppers useful recommendations they can compare before deciding what to buy.

extracts.label: From the introduction
extracts.text: Poetry lovers are notoriously difficult yet wonderfully rewarding to buy for. They rarely want disposable novelties; they crave things with depth, texture, and emotional resonance. Here are ten tactile gift ideas crafted for the sentimental and the overthinkers:

sample.notes: The recovered Semrush UK research (25–26 November 2026) estimated 70 monthly searches for “poetry gifts” and 30 for “gifts for a poetry lover”, both with informational intent. The guide mixes studio products with independent recommendations. Product links give readers a next step once they recognise an idea that suits the recipient.

extracts.text:
Some things are easier to write than to speak.

Almost, Always. is a poetry-inspired hardcover journal from Cold Feet Editions, created for the thoughts that linger, the conversations we rehearse and the feelings we haven't quite found the language for.

extracts.label: From the product details

Size: 5.2 × 7.4 inches (approximately 13.2 × 18.8 cm)

writing.title: Lessons in Anatomy
writing.description: An original poem that moves from a hazy horizon and an immortal jellyfish to the salt the sea leaves on your fingertips.

image.alt: Original Lessons in Anatomy poetry print with a hand-drawn jellyfish, handwritten lettering and ink-wash waves

sample.audience: Readers of contemporary poetry and literary artwork.
sample.objective: Give an unresolved feeling a physical presence through the movement of the sea and the salt it leaves behind.
sample.notes: The poem begins at a distance, with a horizon and boats, then moves close enough for the sea to touch skin. The immortal jellyfish opens a question about what it means to endure suffering. The joke about its missing heart gives that question a darker edge. By the end, the sea asks forgiveness and the salt speaks, giving an unfinished conversation a voice.

lines: You sit your jaw on the horizon haze,
look at where boats float over deep water
and think about all the fish that look up
from underneath and cry.
Scientists have just discovered
the world's first immortal jellyfish,
You wonder if it knows it,
wonder if it knows its own agony.
You say that it's nature's last funny joke;
the first immortal creature doesn't have a  heart.
The sea creeps over your feet,
asking for forgiveness in the sound it makes as it leaves.
It turns suffering touchable,
the salt clinging to your fingertips says,
“I think we have unfinshed business,
and I think you know it.”

sample.adaptation: The original poem was later adapted into an illustrated short film.

writing.title: A Whole Lungful of Nostalgia
writing.description: An original poem about memory, distance and home, told through small gestures of closeness and the sound of a departing train.

image.alt: A Whole Lungful of Nostalgia poetry print with handwritten lines and a steam train in a snowy landscape

sample.audience: Readers of contemporary poetry and literary artwork.
sample.objective: Capture how closeness lingers after departure through the everyday details that memory holds onto.
sample.notes: Short fragments gather a place and a relationship through details such as fold-up beds, cold fingers and an eyelash. The repeated warmth moves from the hands to the heart, connecting physical care with the feeling of home. The sound of the train gives way to a repeated question, as though the speaker is asking someone else to see what memory is holding in view.

related.label: See the visual identity and product design

lines: Blankets of snow, smattering,
cross country landscape differences.
An old home. Something grown.
Intellectualising emotions.
Laughter crinkled eyes hiding worried multitudes.
Superman costume.
Not hiding anything, not really.
Head on my shoulder, fold up beds,
holding my hands between yours like a promise,
blowing warmth back into my fingers.
Breathing warmth back into my heart.
Learning that distance has nothing to do with being apart.
A whole lungfull of nostalgia.
Somewhere where love has always been on my side.
Once in a lifetime hopes. A need for closeness, always.
Hangover headaches, suns rainbow refractions.
Finding an eyelash on your cheek and using the wish for myself.
The sound of the train leaving,
Can you see it?
Can you see it?
Can you see it now?
